title: The golden deer
hookLine: Maricha becomes a golden deer, and Rama chases it; maya
carry: maya dazzles, and isn't what it seems
last: AHAMKARA: THE EGO SHOUTS OVER WISDOM.

lines: DIE BY RAMA, OR BY ME.
cards: Ravana tells Maricha the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want it.
Rama will chase it. While he's gone, I'll take her. Maricha begs him not to; he's felt Rama's arrow once.
Ravana gives him a choice: help me and maybe die by Rama's hand, or refuse and die by mine right now. Maricha makes a grim calculation: if I have to die, better it's by Rama. So he goes.
One morning at Panchavati, a deer steps out of the trees. It's golden. Its spots shine like silver.

teach.b: Sita is picking flowers when she sees it, and she's delighted. Catch it for me, she tells Rama. Alive, or for its golden skin.
Lakshmana says what's true: there's no such thing as a golden deer. This is Maricha. It's a trick.
But Sita wants it, Rama wants to give it to her, and the deer is right there, shining. So Rama picks up his bow, tells Lakshmana to guard Sita and not leave her for anything, and goes after it.
Close, then gone. Close, then gone. Look at how the trap works.
It didn't need force. Ravana put something beautiful where it would be seen. Readers sometimes blame Sita for wanting the deer.
The tradition is gentler: it catches Rama too, who knew better.
That's why the golden deer is one of Hinduism's great pictures of maya, your eighteenth word.
Teachers explain maya in different ways, but here's the heart of it: the world's shine can pull you away from what's real and lasting, God, the people you love, your dharma.

teach.h: MAYA DAZZLES, AND ISN'T WHAT IT SEEMS.
teach.b: Maya dazzles, and isn't what it seems. Now look back at this week. A king's old arrow came home.
A brother bowed to sandals. A family lived the forest stage early. One harm fed the next.
God came down with a bow. A brilliant king's ego won. And a deer too beautiful to be real walked out of the trees.

how: Hindus often use the golden deer as a picture of maya, the dazzling appearance that misleads; the scene is a favorite in Ramlila, painting and children's retellings.

the demon who took the shape of a golden deer

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: die by Rama, or by me

s: Maricha happily agrees to Ravana's plan
he begs him not to, and goes only when Ravana threatens to kill him.
Lakshmana warns that the deer is a trick
there's no such thing as a golden deer, he says. it's Maricha.
the golden deer is a picture of maya
something that dazzles and isn't what it seems.

games.q: you're Rama. your wife wants the golden deer, and your brother says it's a trick. what do you do?
o: take your bow, leave Lakshmana to guard Sita, and chase it.
games.why: he goes after it. the deer leads him deep into the forest, close, then gone.

practice: Think of something you want right now that shines a little too brightly: a purchase, a person, a promotion, a scroll that never ends.

Picture it in front of you like the golden deer and notice how it pulls, without judging the wanting. Then ask Lakshmana's question: is this real, or is it maya? If you pray, ask God to help you see what's real.

wordCard.voice: Maricha, the demon in disguise, sent by Ravana as a beautiful golden deer that leads Rama away from the hut.

orig.note: Sanskrit: deer, or any wild animal of the forest.

carryVoice: Your line: maya dazzles, and isn't what it seems. The deer only had to shine. Day forty-nine: seven full weeks.
